attributes.action: Extend Bereavement Support Payment to all unmarried partners after five years
attributes.additional_details: Couples can share their lives, homes and finances for decades without marrying. Yet someone married for just weeks may qualify for Bereavement Support Payment, while an unmarried partner of 10/20 years without children may receive nothing. We think this is unfair and believe couples who have lived together for at least five years should qualify, with evidence such as shared bills, addresses or finances. In our view, bereavement support should recognise genuine, committed relationships, not just marriage certificates.
attributes.background: Change the eligibility rules for Bereavement Support Payment so that all unmarried partners who have lived together in a committed relationship for at least five years can qualify for payments, regardless of whether they have dependent children.

other_parliamentary_business.body:
The MPs on the Petitions Committee have scheduled a debate on the following petition:

Raise Bereavement Support Payment and extend beyond 18 months
https://petition.parliament.uk/petitions/752501

The debate will take place on Monday 23 November at 6pm. Irene Campbell MP, a member of the Petitions Committee, will open the debate.

Share your views

To inform the debate, you can answer our survey[1].

Deadline: 10am on Tuesday 10 November

Your responses will be anonymous. A summary of responses will be published on the Parliament website. It will also be shared with MPs and may be referred to in the debate or within other parliamentary documents. Please don't share any personal information that may identify you.

What are petitions debates?

Petitions debates are ‘general’ debates which allow MPs from all parties to discuss the important issues raised by one or more petitions, and put their concerns to Government Ministers.

Petition debates don’t end with a vote to implement the request of a petition. This means that MPs will not vote on the request of the petition at the end of the debate.  

Get involved in the work of the UK Parliament

Sign up to the Your UK Parliament newsletter[2] for the latest information on how to get involved and make a difference.
